reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive platelet function disorder caused by quantitative or qualitative deficiency of the platelet integrin alphaIIbbeta3 (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa) fibrinogen receptor
Because the final common pathway of platelet aggregation is defective, platelets fail to bind fibrinogen and cannot form a stable aggregate
Bleeding is mucocutaneous: easy bruising, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and menorrhagia, often presenting in infancy or early childhood
Platelet count and morphology are normal, which helps distinguish it from thrombocytopenic causes of bleeding
Light transmission aggregometry shows absent aggregation to all physiological agonists (ADP, collagen, thrombin, arachidonic acid) but preserved agglutination with ristocetin
Flow cytometry demonstrating reduced or absent surface CD41/CD61 confirms the diagnosis and can distinguish it from Bernard-Soulier syndrome

Management principles include local haemostatic measures, antifibrinolytics, hormonal control of menorrhagia, and platelet transfusion for severe bleeding, reserving transfusion to limit alloimmunisation
Repeated platelet transfusion risks alloimmunisation against HLA and against alphaIIbbeta3, which can render future transfusions ineffective
Recombinant activated factor VII is used as a haemostatic option in refractory or alloimmunised patients
reference.pathophysiology: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by mutations in the genes encoding the alphaIIb or beta3 subunits of the platelet integrin alphaIIbbeta3 (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa). This integrin is the receptor through which platelets bind fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor to cross-link with one another during aggregation, the final common step of primary haemostasis. Absent or dysfunctional receptor prevents platelet-to-platelet bridging, so a stable platelet plug cannot form despite normal platelet numbers, adhesion and initial activation. The result is a lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding tendency of variable severity that does not correlate closely with residual receptor levels.
additionalDifferentials: Bernard-Soulier syndrome and other inherited platelet function disorders
Mild forms of haemophilia or other coagulation factor deficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Platelet aggregometry showing absent response to physiological agonists with intact ristocetin agglutination
Flow cytometry for platelet surface glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (CD41/CD61) expression
Full blood count and blood film to confirm normal platelet number and size
Molecular genetic testing of ITGA2B and ITGB3
Screening for platelet alloantibodies in previously transfused patients
redFlags: Severe or life-threatening haemorrhage (gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding)
Bleeding refractory to transfusion suggesting platelet alloimmunisation
Major surgery or delivery without a planned haemostatic strategy
reference.prognosis: With modern supportive care most patients have a good life expectancy, though bleeding episodes can be severe and occasionally life-threatening. The main long-term challenges are managing recurrent mucosal bleeding and menorrhagia and avoiding platelet alloimmunisation that limits transfusion efficacy.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal platelet count excludes a serious inherited bleeding disorder
Transfusing platelets liberally and precipitating alloimmunisation
Overlooking iron deficiency from chronic mucosal or menstrual blood loss
Giving antiplatelet drugs or NSAIDs that further impair haemostasis
Failing to plan peri-procedural cover before surgery or childbirth
